chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
title: Lester Young and his intentional shock
summary: Butler first heard Lester on clarinet in Moten's band, discusses Herschel Evans, Chu Berry and Don Byas, and sees Lester as an intentional shocker and individualist younger than Hawkins.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Well, what you were saying, how did Young strike you when you heard him, first heard him?

Well, Lester Young struck me as a -- first, I heard him play the clarinet. See, I heard him play in Moten's band the clarinet and I heard him -- Herschel Evans play the tenor saxophone. And Herschel Evans, see, Herschel Evans had lived what it seemed like, because Chu Berry had been around there and Don Byas had been around there a long time. And before Don Byas died, he was playing all of that complete music, because he went and stuck to a course of harmony and theory. He was a valedictorian. When he come out of there he was playing all types of stuff.
So, Lester Young, he struck me first, he was, he had decided that I'm going to shock people intentionally.

See, you got to watch to see what the man is doing. See? So, I'm going to shock them intentionally. And he knows what he's doing. And he doesn't want to follow nobody. He's an individualist. And I accept him as that.
I accept him as that. And he was a younger man than Coleman Hawkins.

He had heard Coleman Hawkins so, that was all. And as I, to my opinion, Coleman Hawkins was the king. Had he -- he should -- in fact, were I he, I would have followed my road as the king, doing what I did to make me king and not followed the road of the crown prince. That is what I felt.
Because later I found that Hawkins was not playing Hawkins, he was playing someone else. And, that's what I heard.I have nothing more to say on that particular subject.
